Determined
de-TER-mind
v. (past part.)
From Latin determinare, to set a boundary or limit, from terminus, a boundary stone. Webster 1828: settled; concluded; fixed; resolved. The etymology is the doctrine: to determine a thing is to set its bounds, which is exactly what Acts 17:26 says God has done with the nations.

Biblical Definition

Determined in the New Testament is used of God’s eternal fixing of events and of a man’s settled resolve, and both belong in the same entry because Scripture puts them in the same book. Paul at Athens: God hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Acts 17:26) — not merely that nations exist, but their eras and their borders, fixed beforehand. Peter at Pentecost applies the same doctrine to the worst act in history: Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain (Acts 2:23). The crucifixion was determined, and the hands that performed it are called wicked in the same sentence; the church prayed the same thing in Acts 4, that Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles gathered for to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done. On the human side, Paul uses the word of his own resolve at Corinth: I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2) — a decision made in advance, against the appetite of a city that wanted wisdom.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DETERMINE as to fix the bounds of; to limit; to settle or decide; to resolve; and derives it from the Latin terminus, a boundary. The primary sense of setting bounds is the sense of Acts 17:26.

expand to see more

DETERMINE, v.t. — To fix the bounds of; to limit; to bound; to confine.

To settle or decide; to end, as a controversy; to conclude.

To resolve; to fix a purpose in the mind; as, he determined to go.

DETERMINED, pp. — Ended; concluded; decided; limited; fixed; resolved.

From Latin de and terminus, a boundary or limit — the boundary stone, which is why to determine is first of all to set an edge.

Key Scripture

Acts 17:26 — "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;"

Acts 2:23 — "Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:"

Acts 4:28 — "For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done."

1 Corinthians 2:2 — "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified."

Ephesians 1:11 — "In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:"

Modern Corruption

Acts 2:23 and 4:28 are the texts that make every attempt to soften the divine decree untenable: the crucifixion was determined before it happened, and the men who carried it out are called wicked for doing it.

expand to see more

Arminian and open-theist accounts of providence both work by loosening the decree — God foresees, or God responds, or God permits within a range. Peter’s sermon will not allow it. Christ was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and in the same clause ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain. Acts 4:28 is if anything stronger, and it is a prayer: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel gathered together to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done. The 1689 Confession states the doctrine in the only way the texts permit: God has decreed whatsoever comes to pass, yet so that neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creature. Both halves are asserted because Scripture asserts both.

The pastoral payoff is enormous and is the reason this doctrine belongs in the pulpit and not only in the classroom. If the worst act ever committed — the murder of the Son of God by religious and civil authority acting together — was determined beforehand and turned to the salvation of the world, then there is no evil in a believer’s life outside the same government. Joseph said it to his brothers, Paul said it in Romans 8:28, and the church in Acts 4 prayed it while under threat and then asked for boldness rather than deliverance. Paul’s own I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ is the human resolve that follows: a man whose confidence rests in a determined counsel can afford to preach an unpopular message.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek horizo (G3724), to mark out by boundaries, to determine — whence horizon; proorizo (G4309), to predetermine, predestinate; krino (G2919), to judge or decide, at 1 Corinthians 2:2.

expand to see more

Greek horizo (G3724) — to mark out with a boundary, to determine, to appoint; Acts 17:26, and of Christ declared to be the Son of God with power (Romans 1:4).

Greek horismenos — the participle at Acts 2:23, rendered determinate.

Greek proorizo (G4309) — to determine beforehand, to predestinate; Acts 4:28, Romans 8:29-30, Ephesians 1:5, 11.

Greek boule (G1012) — counsel, deliberate purpose; the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God.

Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to decide, to resolve; I determined not to know any thing among you (1 Corinthians 2:2).

Usage

"Hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Acts 17:26) — nations bounded by decree."

"By the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God… by wicked hands (Acts 2:23) — both halves in one sentence."

"I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 2:2) — a preacher’s settled resolve."
